content: The comprehensive package for addressing substance abuse and improving access to HIV prevention, treatment, and care for individuals who inject drugs is outlined in the Technical Guide for Countries to Set Targets for Universal Access to HIV Prevention, Treatment, and Care for Injecting Drug Users (2012 revision). This guide emphasizes the importance of reliable liver fibrosis assessment when deciding on therapy initiation for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Historically, liver biopsy was considered the gold standard for staging fibrosis, but it is costly, carries risks such as bleeding, and requires expert histological interpretation. Recognizing these limitations, the Guidelines Development Group assumed that liver biopsy would not be feasible in many countries where these guidelines are applied. Instead, non-invasive tests like APRI, FibroTest, FIB-4, and transient elastography (an ultrasound-based technique) are recommended. However, these tests are less accurate than liver biopsy, have variable cut-off values for fibrosis stages, and transient elastography is expensive. Based on a systematic review of test performance and cost considerations, APRI and FIB-4 were deemed more suitable for resource-limited settings. If transient elastography is available and affordable, it is also recommended. Patients with less advanced fibrosis respond better to treatment, while those with advanced disease face higher risks of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Treatment recommendations are based on balancing the benefits (cure, reduced risk of cirrhosis and cancer) against potential harms (drug toxicity and cost). In resource-limited settings, treatment availability is often restricted, necessitating prioritization of patients with advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis (METAVIR stages F3 and F4). If resources allow, patients with less advanced fibrosis (F1 and F2) may also be considered for treatment. HCV treatment is challenging in lowand middle-income countries due to high costs, the need for sophisticated laboratory testing, and the adverse effects of existing medications like interferon and ribavirin. Consequently, treatment rates are low, even in high-income countries, where certain groups, such as current or former drug injectors, are often denied treatment. Standard interferon (IFN) is still used in some countries due to its lower cost, despite being less effective than pegylated interferon (PEG-IFN). The Guidelines Development Group evaluated the benefits of HCV treatment and made recommendations on existing medicines. Four key topics were considered: (i) the utility of treatment versus no treatment, (ii) the efficacy of PEG-IFN versus standard IFN (both with ribavirin), (iii) the efficacy of direct-acting antivirals (telaprevir, boceprevir, simeprevir) combined with PEG-IFN and ribavirin for genotype 1 infection, and (iv) the efficacy of sofosbuvir with ribavirin or PEG-IFN/ribavirin for genotypes 1–4. Evidence shows that treatment with IFN or PEG-IFN combined with ribavirin is significantly more effective than placebo in achieving sustained virological response, even in children, HIV-infected individuals, and people who inject drugs. WHO recommends that all adults and children with chronic HCV infection, including people who inject drugs, should be assessed for treatment. PEG-IFN with ribavirin is superior to standard IFN with ribavirin, offering higher sustained virological response rates without increasing side effects. Therefore, WHO recommends PEG-IFN with ribavirin for treating chronic HCV infection over standard IFN with ribavirin. For genotype 1 HCV infection, treatment with approved direct-acting antivirals (telaprevir, boceprevir, or simeprevir) in combination with PEG-IFN and ribavirin is recommended over PEG-IFN and ribavirin alone. Genotyping is essential before selecting the appropriate regimen. Additionally, patients with genotype 1a treated with simeprevir/PEG-IFN/ribavirin require testing for the absence of the Q80K mutation, as its presence reduces treatment efficacy. For genotypes 1, 2, 3, or 4, treatment with sofosbuvir and ribavirin, with or without PEG-IFN, is recommended depending on the genotype. However, there is insufficient data to recommend one direct-acting antiviral over another, as available evidence comes from drug registration trials without head-to-head comparisons. Safety data for newer compounds are also limited due to the small number of patients treated with these medicines. The high cost of HCV treatment remains a significant barrier. Prices range from $2,000 in Egypt for 48 weeks of PEG-IFN/ribavirin to $84,000 in the US for a 12-week course of sofosbuvir. Efforts to reduce medicine prices are critical, drawing on the experience with HIV treatment, where prices were drastically reduced through generic drug production, voluntary licensing, tiered pricing, and compulsory licensing. HCV screening is essential, as most infected individuals remain undiagnosed. National testing policies and increased investment in screening services are needed, particularly in high-prevalence populations. The introduction of newer direct-acting antivirals offers an opportunity to simplify laboratory requirements, as these medicines are effective across all genotypes and have improved safety profiles, reducing the need for extensive monitoring. Expanding HCV therapy requires decentralizing treatment from specialized centers to primary care clinics, with general practitioners and healthcare workers trained in HCV management. Prioritizing patients for treatment is crucial, focusing on those with advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis (METAVIR F3 and F4 stages). This prioritization may evolve as safer and more effective medicines become available and affordable. People who inject drugs are at high risk of HCV infection due to contaminated injection equipment. Comprehensive harm reduction strategies, including needle and syringe programs and opioid substitution therapy, are essential for prevention in this population. These WHO guidelines aim to support the development and expansion of HCV treatment programs, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. They provide evidence-based recommendations for screening, care, and treatment, emphasizing the continuum of care as a critical component of HCV management. The guidelines will be revised in 2016 to incorporate new medicines and interim guidance will be issued as needed.
